job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Umar Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I get up around eight and walk to a coworking space in Pinheiros, in São Paulo, where Pagueli, a payments startup of twenty-five people, rents a floor. I'm a junior backend developer: I write the code that moves money between accounts and fix whatever breaks. I use an AI assistant for almost everything, writing, explaining and testing. I studied computer engineering and got a plain pass with no internship, but I built websites for small shops at weekends. I share a flat with my friends Caio and Bia, and my mum calls every evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's a relief for the market and a bit of a letdown for me. I like the tools, they save me hours, but a plateau means they'd stay a good assistant. At work I'd say fine, we keep shipping. Online I'd post a meme about hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job is fine but the company isn't certain. Pagueli has about eighteen months of money left, and if the funding doesn't come, twenty-five of us are on the street, no AI needed. If AI is just a fancy autocomplete, the thing I worry about is whether my startup survives its next funding round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep coding, save 600 reais a month, and keep my freelance work going at weekends. I'd keep my CV fresh in case Pagueli runs out of money. And I'd keep using the assistant, because it makes me faster than the other juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Slight boredom, slight stress about the funding. Mostly fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know if the funding was going badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My boss Renata would stop talking about next year. Last time, in the spring, she cancelled the team lunch and said it was a budget thing, and half the team updated their profiles that week. I'd probably be the second to notice, after my colleague Davi.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the freelance work if you lost the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Turn it into my main income for a few months, which is thin but possible. I get about 1,500 reais a month from two small shops now, and I could double it if I advertised. It wouldn't pay my rent share, but it would pay the groceries.

say: I'd say it's a relief for the market and a bit of a **letdown** for me.
At work I'd say fine, we keep shipping.
think: My job is fine but Pagueli has about **eighteen months** of money left.
If funding fails, twenty-five of us are out, with no AI needed.
do: Keep coding and save **600 reais** a month.

Keep my CV fresh and keep using the assistant.
feel: Fine, with slight boredom and a **funding** worry in the background.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say finally, this is the moment for people who use the tools. At work I'd say let's use AI more, not less. I'd tell friends it'll be messy and we should sort out the rules, like who's responsible when the AI makes a mistake in a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own work is what the tools do best. Writing code, checking it, explaining it. A junior who just writes simple code is the first to be replaced, and I'm that junior with extra tools. I could be the one who knows how to use them well, or I could be the one competing against them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the heavy tools properly: how to design a system, how to review AI code, how to find the one wrong line in a thousand. I'd ask Renata to give me small projects from end to end, so I'm not just a coder. I'd save 600 reais a month and grow the freelance work as insurance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but excited. It's like surfing: a big wave is exciting until you misjudge it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the skill you think matters most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Judgement. The tool will write anything you ask, so you need to know what to ask and spot when it's wrong. In payments, a wrong decimal is a real person's rent, so judgement matters more than speed. That's slow to learn, which is why I'd want end-to-end projects with Renata.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think loses most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Juniors who only do what they're told, and older developers who say it's a fad. My colleague Davi is 45 and refuses to use it. He's good, but I think he'd be one of the first to go, and I'd feel sad about it.

say: I'd say this is the moment for people who use the tools, and we should sort out who is **responsible** for errors.
At work I'd say use AI more, not less.
think: Writing and checking code is what the tools do best, so simple **junior code** goes first.

do: Learn **system design** and how to review AI code.
Save 600 reais a month and grow the freelance work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be a mess, and governments are not ready. I'd say we need a basic income and quick retraining. At work I'd say nothing, because Renata would be panicking about funding too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is too short for me to become senior. By 2028 an AI writes the code I write, only cheaper. I'm a plain-pass junior with a freelance side hustle, and I'd be up against everyone who is better than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything into the freelance work and into one area where being human matters, like talking to clients and understanding their business. I'd save 800 reais a month, cut out going out, and move in above my parents' bakery if I had to. I'd also learn what robots will do from 2031, because there will be work around that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'm adaptable, so I think I'd find something, but I'd be doing it in a hurry, and hurry is expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does hurry cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mistakes. If I take the first job, I might end up in a worse one. If I wait too long, I'd have no money. The difference between choosing and being pushed is huge, and two years makes it feel like I'm being pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your mum say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd tell me to come home and help at the bakery, and I'd say I would, for a while. She'd feed me, and she'd check my CV, which is a bit scary because she once corrected my grammar on a job application. I'd go back, but I'd see it as a pit stop.

say: I'd say it's going to be a mess, and we need a **basic income** and quick retraining.
At work I'd say nothing, since Renata would be worrying about funding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is a chance. I'd say let's learn quickly and spread the gains. At work I'd propose projects that use AI in payments, with clear checks. I'd tell friends to start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be well placed. I use AI daily, and I'm already freelance. By 2031 I'd be 27 with five years of experience, probably running small projects. I'd be one of the people who knows how to work with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save 700 reais a month, grow the freelance work into a small agency with a friend, and learn systems design. I'd also study how to build things that use AI safely, because that's where the jobs will be. If Pagueli folds, I'd go freelance full time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, a bit thrilled. It feels like being early to something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the risk in being early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it doesn't go the way I think and I've bet on the wrong skills. But I'd rather be wrong early than late, because the skills of understanding systems and clients are portable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your plan be for the robots in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Watch the hands-on side. Delivery, warehouses, factory work: robots come into those in 2034, and my payments code will be part of how they're paid for. So I'd keep one foot in that world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is plenty. I'd say let's use it to retrain people and fix education. At work I'd say let's be patient. Online I'd joke that I'd be retired at thirty-two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine. By 2036 I'd be 32, probably running a team or my own firm. The AI will have changed everything, but I'd have changed with it. My worry is my mum's bakery and the cost of living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and freelancing, save 600 reais a month, and put a little into a small index fund. I'd help my mum modernise the bakery's ordering, using AI. I'd also take a part-time master's in finance, because payments and money are the interesting part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Ten years sounds like a long runway for an adaptive person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd regret doing too slowly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Saving. When I'm calm, I spend. I'd want a rule: a fixed amount moves out the day my pay arrives, so I don't have to decide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do for your mum's bakery?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Set up online orders, a simple stock tracker and an AI to answer customers on WhatsApp. It'd take me a weekend and save her about two hours a day. Small businesses might be the winners if the tools get cheap, and my mum's bakery could be one of them.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one, because the code I write is what AI does first and I'd have no time to become senior. What would help is a quick, real retraining system and a basic safety net, plus clients who still pay for judgement. Funding at Pagueli would help too, but that's a different question.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people tend to guess wrong. I've seen the tools change three times in two years, and each time the experts were off. So plan for several futures and don't be loyal to one.

headlineQuote: I've seen the tools change three times in two years, and each time the experts were off.
portrait: **Umar**, 22, is a junior backend developer at a São Paulo startup, with a plain degree and **freelance work**.
A centrist and daily AI user, he treats change as something to ride and trusts **judgement** over speed.
His job is the kind AI does first, but his freelance income and his mum's **bakery** give him a cushion.
He turns anxious at two years and calm when he has five or ten, because time lets him choose.
biggestWorry: The **2028** picture, with little time to become senior before AI does his work.
whatWouldHelp: Real, quick **retraining** and a basic safety net.
Clients who still pay for **judgement**, plus funding for his startup.
